title: Technology and worship
hook: prayer apps, online Qur'an, and the need for real presence

segments.voice: Yesterday, mental health and faith: prayer and therapy side by side. Your line was heal the heart two ways. Whose wellbeing did you check on? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

The app chimes. 'Asr, it says, and a little compass on the screen swings around to point toward Mecca. Useful. The mat goes down, the phone goes down beside it, face up, and the prayer begins. Second rak'ah, forehead on the floor, and the screen lights up: a name, half a message. The prayer carries on. The mind doesn't, quite. Muslims today can carry a prayer timetable in a pocket and open the Qur'an with a tap. Today asks what that does to a prayer, and an old report in al-Bukhari turns out to fit this moment.
screen: `THE APP CHIMES FOR 'ASR.` → `THE SCREEN LIGHTS UP MID-PRAYER.` → `AN OLD REPORT FOR A NEW MOMENT.`

segments.voice: The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aisha. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once prayed in a garment with markings on it, a patterned cloth, and during the prayer his eye caught the pattern. When he finished he said, in paraphrase: take this to Abu Jahm and bring me his plain one, because this one just distracted me in my prayer. Right beside it, al-Bukhari keeps a second report, about a curtain with pictures hanging in 'Aisha's house. The Prophet asked for it to be taken down, because its pictures kept coming to him while he prayed. Notice what he did, and what he didn't. He didn't give up clothes, or curtains. He swapped the one thing that kept pulling at his attention for something plain. The tool stayed. The distraction went. The Qur'an has a word for what was being protected. The chapter called The Believers opens, in Pickthall's translation: "Successful indeed are the believers / Who are humble in their prayers." Muslim teachers call that humility in prayer khushu': stillness, lowered eyes, the whole person turned one way. And in the conversation with the angel Gabriel, the Prophet describes ihsan, doing a thing beautifully, like this, in paraphrase: to worship Allah as though you see Him, and though you don't see Him, He sees you. That is presence. So the question about technology turns out to be an old one. An app that tells you when Maghrib comes is a timetable. A screen that shows the Qur'an is a page. Both can serve the prayer. The question 'Aisha's report asks is simpler and harder: what keeps coming to you while you pray, and can you hand it to Abu Jahm?
screen: `A PATTERNED GARMENT, HANDED BACK.` · `A CURTAIN TAKEN DOWN.` · `THE TOOL STAYS. THE DISTRACTION GOES.` · `KHUSHU': THE WHOLE PERSON TURNED ONE WAY.` · then, large: `AS THOUGH YOU SEE HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: put the phone somewhere else. If it's in your hand, set it down in another room, or at least face down and out of reach, and come back. Settle, and breathe. Notice whether there's a pull toward it, an itch to check. You don't have to fight it. Just notice it, the way the Prophet noticed the pattern on the cloth. Then let your attention come back to one thing: your breath, the room around you, or, if you pray, the words of al-Fatiha said slowly in your head. When the pull comes again, notice it again, and come back again. The bell holds the time.
Technology and worship. Apps, screens and timetables that can serve a prayer, and the presence that no tool can supply. Today's word.
Your line: real presence. Today, for one prayer, one meal or one conversation, leave the phone in another room. Tomorrow, social media and the tongue. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-two.

screen: `DAY 1392 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SOCIAL MEDIA AND THE TONGUE.`

howItsDone: Muslims today may use apps or printed timetables for prayer times and the direction of the qibla, and some put the phone on silent or in another room before they pray.

fork.setup: you're praying in a new patterned garment, and the pattern keeps catching your eye. the prayer ends. what do you do?
options: stop wearing anything that could ever distract.
give it away and ask for a plain one.
keep it, and just try harder not to look.
fork.reveal: the Prophet sent it to Abu Jahm and asked for his plain garment, saying it had distracted him in prayer. the cloth went; the clothes stayed.

original.note: Arabic: humble stillness and full attention in prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: phones are a brand-new problem for prayer.
what it means: the tool can stay. what goes is whatever keeps pulling the heart away while you pray.
what a scholar hears: khushu', the humble attention of 23:2, and two reports in al-Bukhari, a patterned garment and a curtain, both set aside because they distracted the Prophet in prayer.

notes: Confirm hadith numbers: Bukhari 373 (khamisa with markings, narrated by 'Aisha, sent to Abu Jahm for his anbijaniyya) and 374 (the qiram/curtain, narrated by Anas). The script does not name the narrator of 374.
Confirm Pickthall's exact wording of 23:1–2, including the line break.
The original note links khushu' and khashi'un (23:2) as related forms of one root; confirm the phrasing.

Phones and prayer apps are not addressed by the sources; the script draws the parallel itself and says so ('the question turns out to be an old one'). A Keeper may want to add how scholars treat reading the Qur'an from a screen.
